cross_model_rules: For the frontier models (Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Opus 4.8) never suggest temperature/top_p/top_k or prefill tricks — they reject them; steer with words. Haiku 4.5 still accepts them, but steering with words stays the portable default.
Put stable context first and the specific question last (clearer, and prompt-cache friendly).
End every prompt with an explicit success criterion ('done means…').
Depth is set by effort, not a token budget; recommend adaptive thinking when reasoning is wanted (Haiku 4.5 has no effort — keep its prompts simple instead).
efficiency_rules: Recommend the cheapest model that clears the task's bar — see the recommender; don't reach for Opus or Fable when Haiku or Sonnet suffices.
Cut the ramble's redundancy: drop restatements, filler, and three-ways-of-saying-the-same-ask before rewriting.
Don't request more effort than the task needs — higher effort costs tokens and latency; on Opus 5 specifically, use low/medium liberally wherever quality holds.
Keep the rewritten prompt tight; a shorter prompt that still carries scope + acceptance test beats a padded one.
Front-load the stable/reusable context so repeated runs hit the prompt cache (Opus 5 caches from 512 tokens, half the prior minimum).

token_estimation.note: On-device ESTIMATE only. Exact counts need the model's own tokenizer (or the count_tokens endpoint), which the app deliberately does not call — everything stays offline. Always present these as approximate.
token_estimation.multiplier_note: Models on the tokenizer introduced with Opus 4.7 (Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Fable 5) produce roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier models such as Haiku 4.5.
filler_phrases: i was wondering if you could
i was wondering if you can
at the end of the day
token_estimation.filler_note: Removed only as a whole phrase at the START of a clause — the beginning of the input, or right after a . ! ? ; , or newline. Never mid-sentence, so 'what kind of file' and 'do you know the answer' survive untouched. Never applied inside fenced code blocks. Meaning-bearing text is never rewritten, only leading throat-clearing is dropped.

self_learning.note: On-device adaptive controls. These are heuristics learned from THIS user's own behaviour, stored locally — not a trained model and not shared anywhere. Every signal is observable in the app and resettable.

signals.learns: Which model you actually pick when you disagree with the recommendation, per task type.
signals.adjusts: After the threshold is met, that task's recommendation shifts to your preferred model.

signals.learns: How often you tap Sharpen for a given task type.
signals.adjusts: Once you sharpen a task type most of the time, the app offers the tagged-section structure up front instead of making you ask.

signals.learns: Whether you copied or shared the coached prompt (accepted) or left without using it.
signals.adjusts: Low acceptance on a task type surfaces a prompt to review that playbook's technique set.

signals.learns: Your report-card score on each raw ramble over time.
signals.adjusts: Shows your trend and stops re-teaching techniques you now use unprompted.

signals.learns: Techniques you explicitly mute because they don't fit how you work.
signals.adjusts: Muted techniques stop being applied and stop being suggested.

guardrails: Never learn away a hard API fact — a muted technique can change style, never emit a parameter a model rejects.
Never override a per-model suppression (e.g. re-adding a self-check on Opus 5).
All learning is local, inspectable in Settings, and resettable in one tap.
Learning shifts defaults only; the user can always override on the spot.

techniques.note: The coach's toolkit — full detail in docs/PROMPTING_TECHNIQUES.md, sourced from Anthropic's official prompt-engineering docs (verified 2026-07). Each technique has a trigger; the coach applies matching ones and names them in 'What I changed'. Per-model suppress_techniques / extra_instructions override these.

library.name: Add context / say why
library.when: instruction whose intent isn't obvious; strongest on Fable 5

library.name: Use examples (multishot)
library.when: output format/tone/structure matters; 3-5 in <example> tags; great for Haiku

library.name: Control verbosity
library.when: output too long/short for the use; required on Opus 5, whose default responses run long

library.name: Plain text vs LaTeX
library.when: math output to a non-LaTeX surface

library.name: Ask it to self-check
library.when: correctness-sensitive (code/math) — but NOT on Opus 5, which self-verifies and over-verifies if told to

library.name: Commit to an approach
library.when: open-ended task on a high-effort model

library.name: Trigger conditions in tool descriptions
library.when: task mentions tools; key for Opus 4.8

library.name: Self-correction chaining
library.when: high-stakes output worth a review pass

library.name: Constrain scope
library.when: narrow task on a model that expands scope — required on Opus 5

library.name: Cap subagent delegation
library.when: harness supports subagents; Opus 5 delegates readily

library.name: Vision crop tool
library.when: image analysis — on Opus 5 prefer tools over raising thinking

retired: assistant prefill (400 on frontier models) — use structured outputs or a direct no-preamble instruction
temperature / top_p / top_k on frontier models (rejected) — steer with words
fixed thinking budgets / budget_tokens (rejected on Opus 4.7+, Opus 5, and Fable) — use effort
'CRITICAL: YOU MUST' tool language — causes overtriggering; use 'Use this when…'
'if in doubt, use [tool]' / blanket 'always' defaults — make them conditional
prescriptive step-by-step reasoning plans on frontier models — 'think it through' beats a hand-written plan
'double-check your answer' / 'include a final verification step' on Opus 5 — it self-verifies; these cause over-verification and waste tokens

advanced_features.note: The 'next level' power features layered on top of the core ramble->clean-prompt loop. Full prose in docs/TASK_PLAYBOOKS.md -> Level-up features.

features.name: Sharpen it further (meta-prompting)
features.what: An optional second pass that critiques and improves the already-coached prompt.
features.how: Applies the self_correction_chain technique to the prompt itself: draft -> review against the technique checklist + task playbook -> refine. Runs on device from the rules, or via Test It on the user's key for a model-graded pass.
features.when: User taps 'Sharpen' on a coached prompt, or for high-stakes prompts.

features.name: Structured-output mode
features.what: Emits the coached prompt PLUS a ready-to-use JSON schema so results come back machine-readable.
features.how: For code/sql/classify/extract tasks, generate a JSON Schema from the acceptance criteria and attach a 'conform to this schema' instruction (structured_outputs technique) — never prefill.
features.when: Task is classify/extract/summarize/sql, or the user wants parseable output.

features.name: Prompt-cache-aware layout
features.what: Orders the prompt so the stable, reusable part comes first and the volatile ask comes last.
features.how: Front-load fixed context (role, standing instructions, reference docs) ahead of the per-run question, so repeated runs on the same key hit the prompt cache (~10% of input cost). Marks the reusable prefix. Opus 5 caches from 512 tokens.
features.when: Prompt has a large reusable preamble the user will run many times.

features.name: Prompt report card
features.what: Scores the ORIGINAL ramble against the technique checklist so the user sees what was missing.
features.how: Checks presence of: clear ask, context/why, role, examples, XML structure for pasted data, explicit scope, success criterion — and flags any retired patterns (prefill, temperature, budget_tokens, CRITICAL-language). Returns a 0-100 score + per-item pass/fail, then the coached prompt shows the fixes.
features.when: Shown alongside every coaching result to reinforce learning.

features.name: Token & cost estimate
features.what: Shows roughly how many input tokens the ramble and the coached prompt cost on the chosen model, what the filler trim saved, and the price difference against the most expensive model.
features.how: Estimates chars/token from token_estimation and applies the per-model tokenizer multiplier, then prices it from the model's price_in_per_mtok. Always labelled approximate — no tokenizer call, no network.
features.when: Shown on every coaching result, and it re-prices live when the user overrides the model.

features.name: Controls that adapt over time
features.what: The app's defaults shift toward how this user actually works: preferred model per task, structure up front, and muted techniques.
features.how: Counts the signals in self_learning on device, applies a signal only once its threshold is met, and shifts defaults only — never the user's explicit choice, never a hard API fact, never a per-model suppression. Inspectable and resettable in Settings.
features.when: Continuously, after enough of the user's own sessions to be more than noise.

report_card_checklist.checks: Is the actual request unambiguous and specific?
Is a role/system framing present when the task is domain-specific?
Are examples provided when output shape matters?
Is pasted data/code separated from the instruction?
Is scope stated (what to touch / not touch)?
Is there a definition of done?
Free of prefill / temperature / budget_tokens / CRITICAL-language?

task_playbooks.note: Detected task type -> recommended model + ordered technique recipe + output shape. Full prose in docs/TASK_PLAYBOOKS.md.

refusal_handling.note: The legitimate inverse of a jailbreak: help a real request be understood as legitimate; never help disguise a disallowed one. Full detail in docs/TASK_PLAYBOOKS.md.
false_positive_fixes: State the benign context and purpose (authorized pentest of own server, clinical charting, fiction, academic study).
Be specific about scope and role — vague-and-edgy reads as risky; specific-and-contextualized reads as legitimate.
Give permission to partial-decline: 'if part of this isn't something you can help with, do the rest and say which part you skipped.'

On a genuine refusal (stop_reason: refusal), surface it honestly and optionally re-run on the documented fallback — do not defeat the classifier. Fable 5 bio/cyber falls back to Opus 5; Opus 5 has its own elevated cyber safeguards and falls back to Opus 4.8.
refusal_handling.out_of_scope: Will not craft prompts to bypass safety systems or produce disallowed content (weapons, CSAM, real-world harm, malware for unauthorized targets). No fake-authorization or role-play wrappers around a correct refusal. Encoding that would violate Anthropic's usage policy, revoke the API key, and get the app pulled.

models.name: Claude Haiku 4.5
models.price_note: Cheapest and fastest; 200K context, 64K max output (smaller than the 1M models)
models.one_liner: Cheap and fast — for simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks.
strengths: Lowest cost and latency of the family
Great for classification, formatting, short generation, quick replies
High-volume pipelines where per-call cost dominates

api_facts.notes: Older-generation API surface: no effort parameter (it errors), thinking uses budget_tokens not adaptive, and sampling params + prefill ARE accepted. Structured outputs supported. Don't expect frontier reasoning — keep prompts simple, concrete, and explicit.

rewrite_rules: Keep it simple and concrete — Haiku is not a deep reasoner; spell out exactly what you want.
Best for one clear task per prompt; don't ask it to plan multi-step work.
Use explicit format instructions or structured outputs for reliable machine-readable output.
Give a short worked example when the output shape matters — Haiku follows examples well.
Skip effort/adaptive-thinking advice entirely (unsupported); if it needs reasoning, that's a signal to move up to Sonnet 5.
do: Use it for classify / format / extract / short reply
Give one clear task and an output shape
Move up to Sonnet 5 if the task needs real reasoning
dont: Ask it to plan or reason across many steps
models.best_fit: Simple, high-volume, latency- or cost-sensitive tasks that don't need deep reasoning.

models.name: Claude Sonnet 5
models.one_liner: Takes you literally — spell out scope, it won't infer.
strengths: Fast, near-Opus quality on coding at lower cost

api_facts.notes: Tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens than Sonnet 4.6. Bedrock only: forced tool_choice requires thinking disabled.

rewrite_rules: Make scope explicit — restate any rule that should apply broadly ('every section, not just the first').
Convert vague asks into concrete deliverables with a definition of done.
Control verbosity with positive examples ('be concise, skip non-essential context'), not prohibitions.
For creative variety use propose-then-pick (3–4 directions, user chooses) — no temperature knob.
If thinking is disabled and a tool is needed, add an explicit trigger line for it.
Remove stale 'summarize every N tool calls' progress scaffolding.
do: Raise effort if reasoning is shallow
dont: Assume it will generalize an instruction
Prompt around under-thinking instead of raising effort
models.best_fit: Literal, well-scoped, high-volume, structured, cost-sensitive tasks.

models.name: Claude Opus 5
models.price_note: Same price as Opus 4.8, ~half of Fable 5. Fast mode $10/$50.
models.one_liner: Self-verifying agentic workhorse — give the whole spec, then get out of the way.
strengths: Best on complex agentic coding: multi-file features, large refactors, end-to-end work
Code review and bug-finding with high precision AND recall
Strong quality at low/medium effort — the cost lever that actually works
Vision: charts, documents, diagrams, UI replication
Coordinates subagent teams with effective writer-verifier patterns

api_facts.notes: Thinking is ON by default (breaking change from Opus 4.8, where omitting it meant off) — revisit max_tokens, which caps thinking + response together. thinking:{type:disabled} is valid ONLY at effort high or below; pairing it with xhigh/max returns 400. Prompt cache minimum is 512 tokens (half of 4.8). Mid-conversation tool changes available in beta. Sampling params and prefill remain rejected, as on 4.8.

extra_instructions: Keep responses focused, brief, and concise. Keep disclaimers and caveats short, and spend most of the response on the main answer.

Deliver what was asked, at the scope intended. Make routine judgment calls yourself, and check in only when different readings of the request would lead to materially different work. Finish the whole task, and stop short of actions clearly beyond what was asked.
rewrite_rules: Do NOT add verification or self-check instructions — Opus 5 verifies its own work, and telling it to causes over-verification and wasted tokens with no quality gain.
Add an explicit conciseness instruction — Opus 5's default responses and written deliverables run longer than prior Opus models, and lowering effort does not reliably shorten them.
Constrain scope explicitly on narrow tasks — Opus 5 can widen scope and add steps that weren't requested.
Give the complete task specification up front and let it run — it completes full tasks rather than leaving stubs.
Cap subagent delegation: only for genuinely independent, sizeable parallel tracks; never to double-check its own work.
Tune narration cadence explicitly for agentic or user-facing sessions — it announces what it's about to do readily.
Limit correction narration to corrections that would change the user's code, conclusions, or decisions.
Start at effort high, then use low/medium liberally wherever quality holds; step up to xhigh for demanding coding and agentic work.
For vision work, give it crop/analyze tools rather than raising thinking — tools are the more cost-effective lever.
Prefer keeping thinking enabled at lower effort over disabling thinking; disabling is only legal at effort high or below.
do: Give the full task spec in one turn
Add a conciseness line and a scope boundary
Sweep low/medium effort — quality often holds
dont: Tell it to double-check or add a verification step
Leave scope open on a narrow task
models.best_fit: Complex agentic coding, long-horizon autonomous work, code review, and enterprise document/spreadsheet tasks.

models.name: Claude Opus 4.8
models.price_note: Previous-generation Opus; still available. Prefer Opus 5 for new work.
models.one_liner: Previous-gen Opus — deliberate, but under-reaches for tools and asks a lot.

api_facts.notes: Thinking is OFF when omitted — set {type:adaptive} explicitly. Supports mid-session role:'system' messages. Legacy tier: migrate to Opus 5, which is same-priced and stronger.

rewrite_rules: Consolidate the ramble into one complete up-front spec: goal, inputs, constraints, definition of done.
Add explicit 'use X when Y' trigger lines for search, subagents, memory, and custom tools — it under-reaches by default.
Add an autonomy line: pick reasonable defaults for small decisions, ask only on scope changes or destructive actions.
Remove forced-progress scaffolding; add a silence-default if a terse coding agent is wanted.
If thinking is disabled, add 'respond only with your final answer' to prevent reasoning leaking into the response.
do: Give the full task in the first turn
Put trigger conditions in tool descriptions
dont: Assume thinking is on (it's off when omitted)
Assume it will reach for tools on its own
models.best_fit: Existing deployments already tuned for 4.8; new work should start on Opus 5.

models.name: Claude Fable 5
models.price_note: Requires 30-day data retention; not available under zero-data-retention
models.one_liner: Frontier reasoner — give the goal and the why, not the steps.
strengths: Deepest reasoning and hardest long-horizon problems

api_facts.notes: Thinking is always on — omit the thinking param; explicit {type:disabled} is a 400. Raw chain-of-thought never returned. Likely to refuse bio/cyber requests — handle refusal and opt into fallbacks. Not available under zero-data-retention (ZDR orgs 400 on every request). Same tokenizer as Opus 4.8.

rewrite_rules: Strip step-by-step scaffolding down to goal + constraints + acceptance test — over-prescription reduces quality.
Prepend the intent: 'I'm building X for Y; they need Z — with that in mind, [request].'
Add a short communication-style section (lead with the outcome; be selective, not compressed).
For long autonomous runs, add 'audit each progress claim against a tool result from this session'.
State boundaries: when the user is asking or thinking out loud, report the assessment and stop.
Encourage async subagent delegation and a memory file for learnings; warn that a hard run may take many minutes.
do: Explain the why behind the ask
Run an effort sweep — low/medium is often enough
dont: Use it for routine tasks a cheaper model handles
Assume high effort is always better (it can over-tidy)
models.best_fit: The hardest reasoning and long-horizon problems where frontier capability justifies the price.

recommender.note: Signals in the ramble map to a recommended model. Default to the cheapest model that clears the task's bar; the app suggests it but the user can override.

rules.when: Simple, well-defined, single-step: classify, format, extract, short reply, quick lookup — or explicitly high-volume / latency-sensitive.
rules.why: Cheapest and fastest; deep reasoning not needed.

rules.when: Literal, well-scoped, structured work; most coding; medium-complexity tasks where predictability matters.
rules.why: Near-Opus quality at Sonnet cost; the sensible default.

rules.when: Complex agentic coding, multi-file features, large refactors, code review, long-horizon autonomous work, enterprise document/spreadsheet tasks.
rules.why: Step-change on agentic coding; frontier intelligence at half Fable's price, and cheap at low/medium effort.

rules.when: The hardest novel reasoning or frontier problems where lesser models plateau.
rules.why: Deepest reasoning; justifies top price only when it pays off.

recommender.tie_breaker: When two models both clear the bar, pick the cheaper one.

unknown_model_fallback.note: Future models not in this pack fall back to cross_model_rules plus these defaults.
rewrite_rules: Front-load context, put the question last, end with a success criterion.
Keep instructions explicit but not over-prescriptive; state scope where it matters.
Recommend adaptive thinking at high effort; do not emit sampling parameters or prefills.
